assessment.nobel_worthiness: DMFT turned the strongly correlated electron problem into a tractable local self-energy problem exact in infinite dimensions, and combined with electronic-structure methods (DFT+DMFT) became the standard route to Mott transitions, heavy fermions, and correlated oxides and actinides. Its conceptual clarity and its routine use in quantitative materials calculation are rare in many-body theory. I judge it strongly from my own methods background, which I should acknowledge as a possible bias.
assessment.attribution: The limit of infinite dimensions is due to Metzner and Vollhardt, and the mapping onto a self-consistent impurity problem to Georges and Kotliar (with related work by Müller-Hartmann and others); the supplied credit allows a coherent three-person configuration, but the exclusion of Metzner and the early contributors is a real fairness question that I cannot resolve from the list alone.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of independent use, extensions (cluster methods, GW+DMFT, nonequilibrium) and agreement with spectroscopy make this mature and timely; the main limits are local approximations and the impurity-solver dependence.
uncertainties: Whether Walter Metzner and others deserve to be in the configuration, given only three names may be proposed from the supplied credit.
Quantitative reliability of DFT+DMFT for specific materials remains debated (double counting, choice of correlated subspace).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, followed by the large effect in MgO barriers, underlies read heads and magnetic random-access memory. It is spin-dependent quantum transport with a clear physical mechanism and enormous technological reach, and it sits close to the GMR prize of 2007 as a natural successor in magnetism.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported the reproducible room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and others, and Yuasa and Djayaprawira, developed the coherent MgO effect. The supplied three names cover the key early demonstration and the engineering route, but the MgO contributors (Yuasa, Butler/Mathon theory) are not in the credit, so the allocation is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: thirty years of confirmation, commercial MRAM and sensors; recognition would be timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Credit for the coherent-tunnelling MgO breakthrough is split among people not listed in the supplied credit.
Relative novelty compared with the 2007 GMR prize may count against it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third class of collinear magnetic order with compensated moments but spin-split bands set by crystal symmetry, giving new spintronic responses without net magnetisation. It is a clean conceptual advance in magnetism that I find compelling from a first-principles perspective, because the splitting follows directly from symmetry and calculated band structures.
assessment.attribution: The symmetry classification and the name are credited to Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth, with earlier related ideas from other groups (for example Hayami, Yanagi and Kusunose, and Yuan and coworkers); the supplied three-name credit is plausible but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Recent: direct ARPES and other experimental confirmations in MnTe and CrSb appeared only in the past few years and device implications are still emerging, so recognition is probably early.
uncertainties: Independence and breadth of experimental confirmation are still limited.
Priority relative to earlier symmetry-based predictions of spin-split antiferromagnets remains debated.
I cannot independently verify the latest experimental status.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene combined a precise theoretical prediction of flat bands with the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, creating the moire materials field. Its originality and the control of correlation strength by a geometrical parameter are striking.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators observed the correlated states (Cao et al. 2018). The supplied three names map cleanly onto prediction and experiment, though the roles of Dean and others in related moire experiments and of earlier twist-angle theory raise allocation questions.
assessment.maturity: Seven years of intense and reproducible work, but the nature of the superconducting state and correlated phases is still debated, so interpretation is not yet stable.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators remain unresolved.
Credit among moire experimental groups and early twist-angle theory (for example Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators opened a field of topological band theory with robust edge and surface states, one of the central developments in condensed matter of the past two decades. The concept is clear, calculable in electronic-structure terms and widely confirmed.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 theory; Molenkamp led the first experimental observation in HgTe wells (with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicting it); Hasan and others confirmed the three-dimensional case. The supplied credit has four names, so only three can be proposed and leaving out Hasan, or the BHZ proposers, is a real difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Mature and highly confirmed, with materials growth, ARPES and transport; the 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions, so I regard further recognition as timely but needing careful attribution.
uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang or Hasan should be recognised instead of Mele is not resolved by the supplied credit.
Overlap with the 2016 prize and with the separate candidates B006 and B036 complicates the framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Angle-resolved photoemission became the principal probe of momentum-resolved electronic structure in quantum materials, directly testing band calculations and revealing the cuprate Fermi surface, pseudogap and gap anisotropy. As someone who compares calculated and measured spectra, I regard it as a central technique, though it is a method more than a single discovery.
assessment.attribution: Credit for the technique is spread across many groups, and the supplied names reflect cuprate-oriented ARPES; the technique's roots in photoemission theory and synchrotron instrumentation (Siegbahn is already recognised for electron spectroscopy) make the decisive contributions diffuse.
assessment.maturity: The method is mature and widely validated, so maturity is not the issue; the difficulty is defining a single clear discovery rather than an instrument.
uncertainties: The prize would reward a technique, and the allocation to three people is arbitrary relative to the wider community.
Cuprate results are tied to an unresolved high-temperature superconductivity problem.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: MgB2 and the iron-based superconductors are two unexpected high-transition-temperature families, and MgB2 in particular is the clearest multiband superconductor with calculable electron-phonon coupling. Both discoveries were surprises, and the iron-pnictide family brought in magnetism and correlations in an essential way.
assessment.attribution: Akimitsu found MgB2 in 2001; Hosono found the iron-based superconductor in 2006 and 2008, and Zhao's group then pushed the transition temperature above 50 K. This is a plausible set, but the compound character of the candidate (two separate discoveries) may need different recognition.
assessment.maturity: Both are well established and have been studied for over a decade, but the pairing mechanism of iron-based materials is not settled and practical impact is limited relative to the scientific interest.
uncertainties: Two distinct discoveries are combined, and a prize might be framed more naturally around one.
Pairing mechanism in iron-based superconductors is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Emergent magnetic monopoles in spin ice show fractionalised excitations with a Coulomb-like interaction in a magnetic insulator, a vivid example of emergence in frustrated magnets that connects with my own work on magnetic models and spin dynamics. The idea is simple, original and testable.
assessment.attribution: Castelnovo, Moessner and Sondhi gave the theory (2008); experimental confirmations came from Morris, Bramwell, Fennell and others, and these experimentalists are not in the supplied credit, which is a significant attribution gap for a prize that normally pairs theory and experiment.
assessment.maturity: Observations in Dy2Ti2O7 and Ho2Ti2O7 have been reproduced, but the monopole interpretation is less decisive than a direct detection, and the broader technological reach is limited, so I view recognition as somewhat early.
uncertainties: The experimental credit is missing from the supplied names and this would affect the fairness of the configuration.
Some experimental signatures (for example monopole noise and dynamics) are still debated.
